title: Storage models and compression
lead: A useful physical layout depends on which parts of the data the workload actually reads.
goals: Compare row, column, and PAX layouts by the bytes read
Encode and decode RLE, delta, and dictionary representations
Distinguish a teaching model from the actual Parquet format

sections.title: The conceptual framework
sections.html:
Updating one order is an example of an OLTP workload, or online transaction processing. A report that totals revenue across millions of orders is an OLAP workload, or online analytical processing. HTAP combines transactional and analytical requirements. The storage layout should suit the parts of the data that each workload usually reads.

A row layout places the fields of one record next to each other. A column layout places many values from the same column together. PAX groups values by column within each page. Parquet organises data into row groups, then column chunks within each group, with pages and metadata inside that structure.

Lossless compression allows the original data to be recovered exactly. Compression can reduce I/O, but compression and decompression require CPU work. Techniques include general-purpose compression, run-length encoding (RLE), delta encoding, bit packing, and dictionary encoding. The examples below work from an original sequence to its encoded values, including subtracting the minimum delta and choosing a bit width for the residuals.

sections.title: An original exercise: which bytes enter RAM?
sections.html:
There are 1,000,000 records of 100 bytes each. A report uses only two fields whose combined size is 12 bytes. Ignore headers, compression, and alignment padding. During a full scan, a row-oriented layout reads approximately 1,000,000×100=100,000,000 bytes, or 100 MB. A column-oriented layout can read just the two required columns: 1,000,000×12=12,000,000 bytes, or 12 MB. Here, 1 MB=1,000,000 bytes.

The reduction is 100−12=88 MB, or 88% of the original 100 MB. The ratio of bytes read is 100/12≈8.33.

Key takeaway

A byte-count ratio of 8.33 does not guarantee an 8.33-fold speedup. The byte-count ratio in this example is approximately 8.33, but execution also includes reconstructing rows from separate columns, decompression, filtering, and other CPU work. The ratio describes the bytes read under the stated assumptions.

If a query retrieves one complete record by id, gathering its fields from separate columns may take more work than reading one contiguous record. For practice, arrange six rows into two row groups of three rows each. Within each group, write column A’s values together, followed by column B’s and then column C’s. Your drawing illustrates a hybrid layout: within each row group, values from the same column sit together.

sections.title: Original encodings you can decode by hand
sections.html:
Run-length encoding (RLE). Start with [7,7,7,2,2,9]. Group each consecutive run of equal values and store (value,count): [(7,3),(2,2),(9,1)]. Compute the sum directly from the runs: 7×3+2×2+9=34. The alternating sequence [1,2,1,2] has no long repeated runs, so metadata may make its encoded representation larger than the original.

Delta encoding. The original sequence is [50,53,54,58,59]. Instead of storing every number in full, retain the first value and the difference between each adjacent pair:

  1. Keep first=50. Calculate 53−50=3, 54−53=1, 58−54=4, and 59−58=1, giving deltas=[3,1,4,1].
  2. The smallest delta is minDelta=1. Subtract 1 from each delta to obtain residual=[2,0,3,0]. A residual is what remains after subtracting the minimum delta.
  3. The largest residual is 3. Two bits represent the unsigned values 0–3, so each residual fits in 2 bits. Decoding still requires first, minDelta, and any necessary metadata.
  4. Add minDelta back to each residual: [2,0,3,0]+1 → [3,1,4,1]. Start at 50 and cumulatively add 3,1,4,1: 50→53→54→58→59.

Dictionary encoding. The sequence [tea,cake,tea,juice] contains three distinct values. Store the dictionary tea→0,cake→1,juice→2. Replacing each value with its code gives [0,1,0,2]. Decode by looking up each code in that same dictionary.

Key takeaway

Dictionary codes do not automatically preserve the original values’ order. Here tea has code 0 and cake has code 1, but cake comes before tea alphabetically. Comparing codes as ordered values is valid only when the code assignment preserves the required order.

sections.title: Capacity practice and the limits of the model
sections.html:
Suppose 1,000 values are all in the range 0–7. The bit-packed payload requires 1000×3=3000 bits, or 375 bytes, compared with 4000 bytes if every number occupies 32 bits. This calculation excludes headers and padding.

Check yourself: what changes if the value 8 appears?

The range 0–8 requires 4 bits per value if the entire block uses one fixed width. The payload becomes 500 bytes. A single exceptional value can change which encoding is best.

These calculations are independently designed exercises, not a standards-compliant Parquet encoder. PDF pages 19–20 introduce the format’s structure; implementing a real parser requires its current specification. Do not assume that every columnar API uses the same file format.

quiz.question: What is the minimum number of bits per unsigned value needed to encode residual=[2,0,3,0]?
quiz.explanation: The largest value is 3, represented as binary 11, which fits in 2 bits.
